Learning Objectives

Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • 01Define and explain the concept of suitability analysis within the context of Geographic Information Systems (GIS).
  • 02Describe the significance of suitability analysis in spatial decision-making.
  • 03Explain the interrelationship between criteria, constraints, and the geographic space in suitability analysis.
  • 04Understand the role of weights in influencing the outcomes of a suitability analysis.
  • 05Work with the essential tools and software used for conducting suitability analysis in ArcGIS.
  • 06Execute the sequential steps in a suitability analysis, including preprocessing, weighting, and final evaluation.
  • 07Interpret the results of a suitability analysis.

Multi-criteria evaluation / analysis (MCE / MCA)

Multi-criteria evaluation (MCE) is a structured approach to evaluating multiple options when making a decision.

Why is it used? Complex decisions often require balancing trade-offs with multiple stakeholders.

Goal: evaluate whether each option meets certain criteria and, based on this, give each option an overall ranking.

What is suitability analysis?

In everyday life we compare houses, jobs, or phones on several preferences. Suitability analysis does the same thing for map locations.

Try it · Where could a new home go?

A small landscape with a hill, a road, and a protected wetland. Tick the criteria one at a time and watch the suitable land narrow. Click any square, or a lettered site, to see how that location scores.

meets all selected misses 1 misses 2 excluded
Criteria
Land meeting every selected criterion—
Site A
That is suitability analysis
A spatial approach to multi-criteria evaluation (MCE/MCA). It qualifies, compares, and ranks candidate locations by how well they meet the criteria we define for a particular goal.

Suitability analysis is useful when:

  • 01There are multiple criteria
  • 02The criteria do not use the same units
  • 03Some criteria are more important than others
  • 04Some areas must be excluded entirely
  • 05Decision-makers want a process that is systematic and explainable

Common applications

In GIS, it is a transparent and systematic way to support location-based decisions, such as choosing land for conservation, urban development, emergency facilities, or commercial uses. It is used across many fields:

Habitat suitabilityCropland evaluationLandfill sitingSolar and wind farm siting Urban developmentMicromobility planningEmergency shelter sitingConservation planning

The overall workflow

Cartographic models combine spatial layers via overlay, buffers, reclassification, and other spatial operations. One example of a cartographic model is suitability analysis, which follows six broad steps:

These steps are often shown in a flowchart because suitability analysis is really a sequence of spatial data inputs and GIS operations.

Step 1

Define the goal

First, define the problem the model is trying to solve. A good suitability analysis starts with a specific question:

  • ·Where is the best place to build a home?
  • ·Which land is most suitable for conservation?
  • ·Where should a new emergency shelter be located?
  • ·What areas are most suitable for solar development?

The goal matters because it shapes every later decision:

Which criteria matterWhat data are neededHow suitability is definedHow the final map is interpreted
Step 2

Identify criteria

Once the goal is clear, identify the criteria used to evaluate each location. There are two important types:

FactorConstraint
What it doesIncreases or decreases the suitability of a locationLimits where the activity can occur
How it actsVaries along a gradientActs as an exclusion
ExamplesSlope, distance to roads, land cost, soil drainage, solar radiationWater bodies, protected areas, flood zones, parcels zoned against development, slopes above a certain threshold

Example: home-site selection

Reasonable criteria for choosing a home site might include:

  • SlopeShould not be too steep
  • AspectSouthern aspects may be preferred for solar warming
  • SoilsShould support septic systems
  • RoadsAccessible, but not too close, for privacy reasons

A strong suitability model does not just list criteria. It explains why each criterion matters and who it matters to.

Group brainstorm · work it out, then raise your hand

We’re siting a new emergency shelter. Name one factor (something that raises or lowers suitability by degree) and one constraint (something that rules an area out entirely). Work it out, then raise your hand.

Factors (gradient): distance to population centers, distance to major roads, elevation above the floodplain, distance from hazards.

Constraints (exclusion): inside a mapped flood zone, on protected/park land, on slopes above a safe threshold, on parcels not publicly owned. The test: a factor makes a place better or worse; a constraint makes it allowed or not.

Step 3

Acquire and prepare the data

After choosing the criteria, we must find and prepare the spatial data. This step may involve:

  • FindVector or raster data sources
  • ProjectInto a common coordinate system
  • ClipTo the study area
  • MatchRaster resolution and extent
  • DeriveNew variables, such as slope or aspect from elevation data
  • ConvertVector layers to raster when raster overlay will be used
  • ReclassifyCategories into usable classes
Step 4

Transform criteria to a common suitability scale

  • ProblemCriteria are measured in different units: slope in degrees, land cost in dollars, distance to roads in meters. These cannot be added directly.
  • FixTransform each criterion to a common scale before combining. They first need to be standardized.
  • ScaleA common choice is a 0 to 1 scale: 0 means not suitable, 1 means highly suitable.

Crisp (Boolean) membership

  • RuleIn a crisp or Boolean approach, a location is either in or out of the suitable set.
  • ExampleDistance from a lake ≤ 0.5 km: assign 1. Greater than 0.5 km: assign 0.
  • Trade-offSimple and transparent, but it can be unrealistic because it creates abrupt cutoffs.

Fuzzy membership

  • RuleIn a fuzzy approach, locations can have partial membership in the suitable set. Suitability is gradual, not all-or-nothing.
  • ExampleAs distance from the lake increases, suitability decreases.
  • WhyThis often better matches real-world reasoning, because many geographic boundaries are vague rather than sharp.
Try it · Crisp versus fuzzy

Five candidate home sites sit at different distances from a lake; closer is more suitable. Move the threshold and the width of the fuzzy transition, and compare the score each site receives under the two rules.

Step 5

Weight and combine criteria

After criteria are standardized, they can be weighted and combined.

  • WeightsRepresent the relative importance of each factor.
  • EffectA factor that matters more for the decision contributes more strongly to the final suitability score.
Weighted linear combination
Suitability = (w1 × factor1) + (w2 × factor2) + … + (wn × factorn)
  • ConstraintsUsually applied afterward, by masking or multiplying the factor-based suitability map so excluded areas become unavailable.
Try it · Weighted linear combination

One candidate site for a new commercial development has four standardized factor scores (0–1, where 1 is most suitable). Move the weight sliders to change each factor’s importance, and watch the combined suitability update. Then flip the constraint to see it masked out.

Combined suitability—

Weighting methods

Several methods can be used to assign weights:

MethodHow weights are setKeep in mind
Equal weightingEach criterion gets the same weightSimple and transparent, but assumes all factors matter equally
Rank ordering / rank sumCriteria are ranked from most to least important, and weights are derived from that rankingUseful if you want to order criteria but not make detailed pairwise judgments
Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)Each criterion is compared with every other in terms of relative importance; the pairwise comparisons build a matrix from which weights are derivedMore structured, and lets us check whether the judgments are logically consistent

Rank ordering / rank sum

Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)

  • ScaleEach judgment asks how much more important the row criterion is than the column criterion, on a 1 to 9 scale: 1 · equal3 · moderate5 · strong7 · very strong9 · extreme
  • ReverseThe opposite comparison is the reciprocal. If parcel cost compared with parking density is 7, then parking density compared with parcel cost is 1/7.
  • WeightsDivide each entry by its column total, then average each row. The row averages are the weights, and they sum to 1.
  • ConsistencyJudgments should not contradict each other. If parcel cost matters more than competitor distance, and competitor distance matters more than parking density, then parcel cost must matter more than parking density. AHP reports a consistency ratio (CR); below 0.10 is acceptable.
Try it · AHP weights for a new commercial development

You are choosing a site for a new commercial development, using the same four criteria as the rank-ordering example. For each pair, choose how much more important the row is than the column. A fraction means the column is more important. The weights and the consistency check update as you go.

Weights
AHP weightrank-sum weight, for comparison
Consistency
Step 6

Locate the most suitable sites

The final suitability surface can be interpreted in different ways, depending on the project. You might:

  • IdentifyThe highest-value cells
  • ClassifyThe surface into low, medium, and high suitability
  • SelectThe top-ranked candidate sites
  • FilterBy parcel size, contiguity, or distance from competitors

The same workflow drives siting decisions worldwide. A few published examples:

Other common applications include landfill siting and habitat conservation. Each has a different goal, but the same six-step skeleton.

The overall workflow: vector analysis is slightly different

  • Same ideasThe key ideas are the same, just slightly simplified.
  • DifferenceWe don’t have the advantage of representing the world continuously, so there is no grid of standardized cells.
  • MethodVector suitability works with overlay of discrete features and their attributes.

Uncertainty in suitability analysis

Suitability analysis is powerful, but it is not objective truth.

Geographic representation is always a simplification of the real world, and uncertainty enters at every step of the workflow:

StepUncertainty enters throughExample
1 · Define the goalHow the problem is defined“Where is the best place to build a home?” Best for a family with school-age children is not best for a retiree. The question has more than one reasonable reading.
2 · Identify criteriaHow criteria are selectedThe commercial development example used four criteria. Another analyst might add foot traffic or drop parking density, and the top-ranked sites would change.
3 · Prepare the dataHow variables are measured; the scale and zoning of the dataSlope from a 30 m DEM is smoother than slope from a 3 m DEM of the same hill, so a site can pass a slope test in one and fail it in the other.
4 · Common scaleHow categories are defined, thresholds are chosen, and suitability is transformedDoes suitability stop at 0.5 km from the lake, or fade out gradually? In the Step 4 explorer at its starting settings, sites B and C scored 1 and 0 under the crisp rule and 0.58 and 0.42 under the fuzzy rule.
5 · Weight & combineHow weights are assignedFor the same four criteria in the same order of importance, rank sum gave parcel cost a weight of 0.40 and the AHP example gave it 0.56.
6 · Locate the sitesHow the result is classifiedCalling cells above 0.7 “highly suitable” instead of cells above 0.8 increases the suitable area, with no change in the data.

Vagueness and ambiguity

Some criteria are uncertain because their meaning is vague or ambiguous:

  • ?What counts as “urban”?
  • ?What slope is “too steep”?
  • ?What counts as “near” a road?
  • ?What density qualifies as woodland?
This is one reason fuzzy membership can be useful: it acknowledges that many spatial concepts do not have perfectly sharp boundaries.

Error vs. uncertainty

It is useful to distinguish between the two:

  • ErrorA measurable difference between a recorded value and a true value.
  • UncertaintyBroader: includes vagueness, ambiguity, and incomplete knowledge.
In class · point & call

Two analysts build the same home-site model from the same data. One treats slopes above 15° as “too steep” and excludes them. The other uses 20°.

  1. Will their two suitability maps agree?
  2. Which analyst made an error?
  3. What should each of them report alongside the map?

1. No. Land with slopes between 15° and 20° is excluded on one map and allowed on the other, so the maps differ wherever such slopes occur.

2. Neither. An error is a measurable difference from a true value, and “too steep” has no true value. Both thresholds are defensible. This is vagueness, a form of uncertainty, not error.

3. The threshold used and the reason for it. Better still, show the map under both thresholds so readers can see how much the result depends on that choice, or use fuzzy membership so suitability declines gradually between 15° and 20°.

Key takeaways

1
It makes trade-offs explicit. Suitability analysis turns multiple criteria and trade-offs into a structured, transparent GIS workflow.
2
The goal drives everything. A clear goal determines which criteria, data, transformations, and interpretations make sense.
3
Factors vs. constraints. Factors change suitability by degree; constraints exclude areas entirely.
4
Standardize before combining. Criteria must usually be put on a common scale before they can be combined, especially when measured in different units.
5
Results are not objective truth. Uncertainty enters through data choices, thresholds, weighting, scale, and vague concepts like “near” or “too steep.”
